title: Latest lab result before each clinic visit
prompt:
A clinic wants each visit summary to show the patient's most recent glucose lab taken on or before the visit date.

For every visit, return the latest lab of the same patient with taken_on <= visit_date. A lab taken on the visit day counts.

- Columns: visit_id, lab_id, glucose
- One row per visit; any row order is fine
- Several labs on the same latest date: pick the highest lab id
- No qualifying lab: keep the visit with NULL lab_id and glucose
- A spoiled sample has NULL glucose; it is still a lab and can be the latest
hints: For each visit you want a top-1 row from another table, chosen by a rule that depends on the visit.
LATERAL lets a subquery in FROM refer to the current visit row, so it can ORDER BY ... LIMIT 1 per visit.
LEFT JOIN LATERAL (SELECT id, glucose FROM labs WHERE patient_id = v.patient_id AND taken_on <= v.visit_date ORDER BY taken_on DESC, id DESC LIMIT 1) l ON true.

exercise.schema:
CREATE TABLE visits (id int PRIMARY KEY, patient_id int NOT NULL, visit_date date NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE labs (id int PRIMARY KEY, patient_id int NOT NULL, taken_on date NOT NULL, glucose int);
exercise.starter:
-- Latest lab on or before each visit
SELECT v.id AS visit_id, l.id AS lab_id, l.glucose
FROM visits v
JOIN labs l ON l.patient_id = v.patient_id AND l.taken_on <= v.visit_date;
exercise.solution:
SELECT v.id AS visit_id, l.id AS lab_id, l.glucose
FROM visits v
LEFT JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT id, glucose
  FROM labs
  WHERE patient_id = v.patient_id
    AND taken_on <= v.visit_date
  ORDER BY taken_on DESC, id DESC
  LIMIT 1
) l ON true;

tests.name: visits with no earlier lab

hiddenTests.name: lab on the visit day counts
same-day labs break ties by highest id
another patient's closer lab is ignored
spoiled sample is still the latest

explanation: LEFT JOIN LATERAL runs the subquery once per visit, and the subquery can use v.patient_id and v.visit_date. ORDER BY taken_on DESC, id DESC LIMIT 1 picks exactly one lab with a deterministic tie-break, and LEFT ... ON true keeps visits that found none. A plain join returns every earlier lab, and joining on max(taken_on) returns duplicates on tied dates. Two scalar subqueries in the SELECT list also work, but each needs the same ORDER BY and repeats the lookup; filtering glucose IS NOT NULL would wrongly skip a spoiled sample.
notes: With an index on labs(patient_id, taken_on DESC, id DESC) each lateral lookup is a short index scan that stops after one row, which beats ranking all labs with ROW_NUMBER when visits are few and labs are many. When most labs are needed anyway, a window function over the joined rows can win, so compare plans. DISTINCT ON (v.id) over the join with ORDER BY v.id, taken_on DESC, l.id DESC is another Postgres-specific answer.
followUps: Return the two most recent labs per visit as an array.
How does the plan change if the index on labs is missing, and when would ROW_NUMBER beat LATERAL?
